utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, a few procedural matters. Mr. Jordash, the scheduling on the 14th of May in the afternoon is definitive, but I hate that I have to say this. And before you take very drastic steps for yourself, the scheduling is there, but if it would turn out that we would have only one witness that week, we might consider to start at 4.00. So much on what actually will happen on the 14th depends very much on the presentation of evidence, and if that would leave sufficient room -- I mean, we would not risk a witness not being able to leave before the weekend, et cetera, but if there is a commitment of the parties and if there is a clear and realistic expectation that even without the first two hours in that afternoon we -- we would not lose anything, then, of course, we would seriously consider that. So therefore, perhaps, you speak about the matters with Mr. Bakrac as well. We are trying to accommodate you to the extent possible, and we'll be very flexible, but Monday afternoon is the scheduled court session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the flexibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Petrovic, as far as the attachments to the report of Mr. Milosevic are concerned, you've used them. Could you include them in the list, at least to the extent you've used them, of source documents so that they receive a number as well, because in e-court they are not part of the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Milosevic, we'll continue. I first would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And when I now invite Ms. Marcus to proceed, I also -- what I have again forgotten yesterday is to introduce Ms. Marcus as counsel for the Prosecution. But again, being a specialist in criminal procedure, you would have noted already that Ms. Marcus was a member of the prosecutorial team in this case. Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you chose to title your report "Discharge of Internal Affairs" because the Serbian language does not provide for another option which would better describe the nature of your study. I would say that a simple title such as "Study of the Rules and Structures of Internal Affairs" might have done the trick, but you are the author, not I. However, I note that throughout your report you continually use terminology which describes not only the applicable rules, laws, and regulations, but which denotes the application of those rules, laws, and regulations. There are scores of examples. To name very few, in paragraph 199 you state that: "The overall financial operations of the RSUP MUP were transacted in the framework of the joint financial service." In paragraph 202: "In accordance with the instructions, the SDB special expenditure resources were used for," and then you say what they were used for. In paragraph 228, you state: "The chief and the leadership of the service department, in the framework of exercising their managerial function, were informed of all the more important primary documents stemming from the operative work of the SDB RDB." You do use conditional language in many places. But in others you chose to use quite concrete and unequivocal terminology. So what -- so that we understand what you are saying about these assertions in your report, any time you use terminology in your report which states that something was carried out or records were kept, rules were applied, all of this we should understand to mean that if the applicable rules had been applied, then this would have been the factual result. But you have absolutely no information about whether or not these applicable rules were, in fact, applied. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the report I provided is quite clear and explicit, and I will leave it to the Chamber to decide about the matter. I don't know how I could now supplement my testimony. Everything contained in this report is quite explicit, and I'll leave the matter in the hands of the Chamber. I'll repeat what I said yesterday, and that is that there were rules of service that were in existence and it was necessary to strictly adhere to all the rules. Failing to do so would entail certain consequences, and therefore I don't know what else I could add.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your report, you state that: "This methodological approach in the expert report, based on the relevant documents ..." You said yesterday that you inspected "personnel files and other decisions including letters of appointments and assignment and the payrolls." Did you have direct access to internal DB documentation in preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What documentation do you actually have in mind? I'm not sure that I have understood your question. What specific documentation do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sure some of my questions will use lay terminology that may not be the official terminology. Please bear with me; I'll do my best. You mentioned, I believe, personnel files, other decisions, including letters of appointments and assignment and the payrolls. I'm trying to determine exactly what those materials were and how you obtained access to them.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we're dealing with are a certain number of decisions on appointments and a certain number of decision on salaries. When someone is assigned to a certain work position, then that person is provided with a decision on the salary and on that position. I had access to such decisions that related to some of the staff members of the anti-terrorist unit. I'm not certain that I saw all the decisions, but I used all the documents I received from the Defence. As for Franko Simatovic's case, well, naturally what I received were photocopies, not originals. I received a photocopy or photocopies of the documents that were contained in his personnel file. And naturally I also examined documents that concerned certain payments made and they were documents that had been assigned, but the key documents for me were documents that concerned individual members of the anti-terrorist unit, because it was on that basis that I established the date of the creation of that unit, because that document officially created the unit. That was in mid-1993, as I have already said. I said yesterday that I haven't seen the original of that document. But I don't think that there is anything that is in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to that issue. I will return to ask you questions about that a bit later. The materials that you say you reviewed, and you said that you "used all the documents I received from the Defence." So all the materials that are these internal DB documents were documents that you received from the Defence; in other words, you didn't obtain access yourself directly through the Serbian authorities to additional documentation. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the documents that are state secrets are not documents that I could have requested access to. I believe that you'll understand that that quite simply wasn't possible. Naturally, I had certain documents at my disposal as a researcher, but these documents aren't confidential. All the documents that concern the RDB were there, were included, and all other documents that I could find were documents I used to draft this report. I can produce a list of the literature I used, if you like. I was involved in all the details. But as far as other documents are concerned, the rules on the organisation and work and on jobs specifications, well, these are state secrets, so I could not have such documents. I could not have access to such documents because in order to have access to such documents I would have had to break the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I intervene. There was a certain category of documents Ms. Marcus referred to and which you mentioned yesterday. The question of Ms. Marcus was whether those documents, that is, appointments, personnel files, et cetera, whether you received those documents exclusively from the Defence or whether you received them also from official sources. And what would violate the law and what not, Ms. Marcus is interested in the facts. Did you receive any of the documents falling in that category from anyone else than from the Defence? That's the question, I think, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please try to briefly answer that question. And not what would have happened if you had asked for other things, just what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The documents that concern the personnel file of Franko Simatovic and that concerned decisions on salaries and assignments of various members of the anti-terrorist units are documents that I received from the Defence, but I have absolutely no doubts as to their authenticity, since the documents are photocopies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes photocopies are not always authentic, but that's not yet in the question of Ms. Marcus. There may be other issues as selectivity, et cetera. But Ms. Marcus -- listen carefully to her next question and try to focus very much on what she asks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, apart from those documents that you actually cited in your report, and apart from the bibliography which you produced for us as well, could you produce for us a list of the documentation that you consulted in preparation of your report that would include all the documents that the Defence asked you -- the Defence provided to you and which you consulted in preparing your report but which we can't find cited in your report. Essentially, those are source -- that's source material for your report which we don't have. Could you provide that list to us if we asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a list of the bibliography of the books that I used and of other secondary material, but there are no other documents. I don't know what you have in mind, exactly. I don't know how I would compile such a list. I have provided everything, and everything has been referenced. If you like, I can go through the material once more, but I really don't understand what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Apart from the personnel file of Mr. Simatovic, which other documents from personnel files, letters of appointment, et cetera, were you provided with by the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were decisions that concerned Milan Radonjic and so on and so forth. If necessary, I can provide you with a precise list. These are standard things. It's just a matter of a sort of textbook example that's provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would, in fact, appreciate if you could at some point -- I don't know how soon you think you could produce that list. With leave of the Chamber, I would request if you could put together that list, the decisions. You said "decisions that concerned Milan Radonjic and so on and so forth." And you mentioned -- you refer to some additional documents of that kind which are not in your bibliography and which are not footnoted in your report. If you could prepare a list for us at some point and provide that, I would very much appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you willing to prepare such a list, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, in the previous version, before the redactions, there was a detailed list of the bibliography. It's not included in the list that the Chamber now has before it. We could, perhaps, provide the Chamber and our colleagues with the original list. In fact, our colleagues from the Prosecution have had it for several months now, but we could provide you with the original list prior to these redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have you looked at the previous version and have you looked at whether a list attached or contained in that would help you out?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have a look at that again. We have looked at it. Can I just understand my colleague Mr. Petrovic: Does that mean that every document that was provided by the Simatovic Defence to the witness in preparation of the report would be contained in that bibliography? Is that my understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's a list of the bibliography that was compiled by Mr. Milosevic. It's his list, his bibliography, and it consists of several pages, of about ten pages if I remember this correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But the question is whether it contains all the material that you have provided to Mr. Milosevic. That was the question. If you don't know, please tell us. If you do know -- or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have to have another look at that list and then provide you with a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milosevic, in an earlier version of your report, the bibliography was far broader, as I understand. In that bibliography of the previous version, had you included a reference to every single document you received from the Simatovic Defence, or would we not find a reference to each and every of those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd have to have a look at it to be able to provide you with a precise answer. I provided a very extensive bibliography, and for certain reasons it was not included. And in that bibliography you can see all the sources that I availed myself of, but I would have to have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because even if you did not use certain documents, you may have received them, you may have considered them, and then not used them. I take it, Ms. Marcus, that that's part of what you would like to know as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing - I'm talking in the -- would you be willing if Ms. Marcus, after having reviewed your bibliography attached to your previous version of the report, would you be willing to make such a list? What Ms. Marcus wants to know is exactly what material you received from the Simatovic Defence. That's what she's -- what she would like to know. I don't know whether you're able, whether you have written it down for yourself anywhere; so, on that I received A, B, C, D, E, because if you don't have that written down, then it might be problematic to produce such a list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At this point in time it's practically impossible, but I can cite the material that I took into consideration. But I didn't use all the material I had because there are these documents, for example, on appointments and there are quite a lot of such decisions. It would be absolutely pointless to reference each of those decisions. But if you like, I can try to do so. I can't do this off the top of my head, though. That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I'll leave it for the time being in your hands. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, for you, Mr. Milosevic: In your bibliography, which is on page 116 of your original report, all that is there are the constitutions, laws, sub-laws, monographs, studies, text books, and articles. There is no DB documentation listed there. So to the extent you are able to piece together as much of a list as possible, the documents pertaining to Milan Radonjic which you just referred to for example, I would very much appreciate that. Now I'll continue. I would think that with your professional background and your experience you would be following this case with great interest. Have you seen the indictment against Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were several indictments. The indictment was amended, wasn't it? I don't know which one you have in mind. I only read the third amended indictment, the last one. I didn't read the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So based upon your consulting the third amended indictment, which is the operative indictment, you do know what the case is about. Would you say that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general. But I didn't go into any of the details because that is not the purpose of my presence here. As an expert witness, I am completely neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up Exhibit P2397, but not broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you will see before you in a moment, Mr. Milosevic, is a decision on the appointment of Jovica Stanisic to the position of assistant republican secretary of the interior, dated the 12th of June, 1990. It says in the first paragraph: "Jovica Stanisic, assistant chief of the State Security Service of the republican secretariat of the interior, is hereby appointed assistant republican secretary of the interior." If we understand this document correctly, Mr. Stanisic, by this decision, was promoted to a higher position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Chief of state security was a position that was at the same time the position of the assistant secretary for the interior. I don't see how he would have been promoted. He shared several positions at the time. That position was also the position of an assistant secretary for the interior. He remained chief of service. He never stopped being chief of service, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. And how did the position of assistant republican secretary of the interior differ from the later position of assistant republican minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the difference was. If he remained in that position -- I'm afraid I don't understand your question. He remained in the position as a chief of service of state security, which later on became the state security department. I can consult my -- the documents. I don't remember that I've ever stated that there was a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 28 of your report, you say: "At the time of the constituting of FR Yugoslavia, the State Security Service, in the federal secretariat of the interior, was nominally organised as ten administrations and two independent departments. However, as of October 1992, actually, and as of 2001 also formally, the federal MUP no longer comprised state security organs." The reason that as of October 1992 actually the federal MUP no longer comprised state security organs, this was because of the Serbian MUP take-over of the federal MUP which we discussed -- which you discussed earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained in my testimony so far that at that moment there were those administrations on paper, but they were completely nonoperational. They existed only on paper, effectively. They didn't have personnel. They were not active. It was a transitional period in the state of chaos that reigned. I've already testified about that. After that, the federal SUP was reorganised. Some administrations remained. But when it comes to state security, everything, save for the protection of individuals, everything was merged, as it were, with the republican ministry of the interior. In other words, that ministry didn't completely disappear. The state security didn't completely disappear. Their activities were significantly reduced, as you will find it stated in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have quite a lot of information, and I have quite a lot of material to cover with you. I'm doing my best to ask quite specific questions. If you would be so kind to please answer as briefly as you can. If I'm asking for a further explanation or if the Chamber would like further explanation, we will certainly ask you follow-up questions. Now, you make very brief mention of this take-over in the one-sentence paragraph 29 of your report, and then you move on from there. You provide no analysis, no assessment of the legality of the circumstances, no presentation of the rules governing the take-over. You did, as you said now, discuss the take-over during your testimony, and you gave a few reasons for it. However, you explained it as some sort of agreed-upon solution to a problem of office space and to "overcome the problem of working on a double-track and duplication that had lead to a lot of unnecessary costs." That's at transcript page 18836. The take-over of the federal MUP by the republican MUP was forcible, was it not?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was your question about the take-over, and did you ask me if it was forcible? You spoke quite at length and then you put a question to me, and I'm just trying to make sure whether I understood the question properly. Did you ask me if the take-over was forcible, and is that the question that I'm supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just give you my personal opinion. Personally I believe that it wasn't forcible because all the employees continued working there. No coercion was used against anybody. There was no force used. To be more precise, I don't have information to the effect that the process was forcible. I didn't find it anywhere in any of the literature that I perused. There was no shooting. There was no force used. There was no violence. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You present it as some sort of a merger or an agreement. And I'm trying to ask you about the circumstances which were, in fact, not pursuant to an agreement. Now, what happened later on may have permitted you to go back and draw a conclusion based on what must have happened, but that's exactly what I'm trying to ask you. This take-over was not pursuant to the rules and it was not pursuant to an advanced arranged agreement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The take-over occurred late on a Sunday evening; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What kind of a major organisation would carry out a merger on a Sunday evening?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In cross-examination leading questions are allowed, but there is no need to comment on the question. Please proceed and please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I'm not familiar with the rules here. As far as your question is concerned, I can only share my opinions as a citizen. I can give you my personal opinions. I've not seen any documents about that, and I couldn't find what the nature and the details of the process were in any of the documents of a more general nature. I really can't testify about that because I never studied this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I request private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You did not directly take part in any high-level Serbian government meetings where the reasons for the take-over were discussed, did you?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In fact, your comments as to the underlying reasons for the take-over are based upon the laws and regulations and the resulting structural changes; correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you deduced from the merger which later occurred what the reasons for the take-over had originally been; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only logical. I was not aware of any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P2993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, this take-over caused a degree of outrage in certain sectors of the government, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. This is the first time I hear any such thing, from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, what you see before you are minutes from the session of the council for reconciliation of standpoints regarding state politics, held just after the take-over on the 2nd of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I please have page 2 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In attendance at this meeting - you can see those who attended; I'll just name a few for the record - Prime Minister Milan Panic; president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic; chairman of the Presidency of the Republic of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic; federal minister of internal affairs, Pavle Bulatovic; and a few others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please have page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to read the paragraphs starting with, "Further on during the session ..." And we will read it as well. Let us know when you are finished, please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have completed reading the passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This meeting describes the republican MUP blocking federal DB employees from reaching their offices, taking over equipment, documentation, registries, essentially rendering the work of the federal DB impossible. This was not an insignificant event, was it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that things evolved that way, that people were blocked. As far as I know, everybody turned up for work on the following day. I accept documents of this kind at their face value. I personally have no knowledge about that. But I'm sure it was a very important event, but I'm not sure that things happened in the way that they are described here. I was not there, so I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The take-over itself was not provided for in any of the rules or regulations, was it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Things like that could not have been provided for. It was a historical moment, one of its kind -- a kind. I don't know how it could have been provided for. But even at that moment it was not understood that something that was against the constitution or negative in any other way. What is mentioned here are some financial problems that were previously mentioned in the press, but I didn't know anything about that. I was not a member of any high-top -- high-level leadership or I was not in the top echelons of the government, so I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the following paragraph of your report, after you make very brief mention of this event, you state that Zoran Sokolovic, the republican minister of the interior, amended the rules on the internal organisation of the DB. So essentially the republican MUP took over the federal MUP building, kicked out the employees, seized all their documents and equipment, lied to the public to cover this up, and then within a few weeks changed the DB rules. Yet you did not consider this a sufficiently significant event to discuss in your MUP expert report.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that had been the case, if those people had been fired, why would then the organisation of work be changed and why would have the list of jobs expanded? And why would then those people have been allowed to come back? I only know that the job specification was expanded after that, and that's all I can testify about. I didn't participate in any of that. I believed that one of the consequences of the take-over was the enlargement of the job specifications. It really doesn't make sense for the employees first to be fired and then asked to come back based on the new job specification. It doesn't make too much sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Milosevic, specifically is: This is an example of a violation of the rules, and in your report, which deals with the rules, you gloss over what I think is clearly a very serious and significant event which blatantly violated the standing rules. That is my question to you. Why did you not expand upon this in your report? Is it because you didn't know about it? You didn't know the details? Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't know what regulations were breached. I didn't know at the time what rules were violated, and that's why I did not refer to that in my report. I did not pay too much attention to that because I thought that it was a fact. I, however, spoke about one of the consequences of the event and that was the passing a new book of rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I am done with this document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 175, you state: "Pursuant to Article 9 of the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, at the request of the National Assembly and the president of the republic, the minister of the interior was required to submit a report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior and on the security situation in the republic, which also included the work of the service department." I'd like to ask you a few questions about this. I hope you won't mind if I sit down for a little bit. From the way this is unequivocally worded, much like in many other places in your report, you appear to have direct knowledge or, at least, you do not cite to any other source for this assertion, that this report also included the work of the service department. Can I take it from the way this is worded that according to your evidence such reports were, in fact, provided by the minister of the interior to the National Assembly and to the president of the republic containing information on the work of the service? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand what's in dispute in this statement. This is based on Article 9 on the internal affairs of the Republic of Serbia. Pursuant to that article, it says explicitly in that article that the Ministry of Interior is duty-bound to report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior. Since the state security department was one part of the Ministry of the Interior as well as the public security, it was implied that that would be comprised within that rule. It was a legal obligation of the Ministry of the Interior. And if the Ministry of Interior violated the law and didn't do that, I don't know. What I'm saying here is that that was his obligation. He was duty-bound to report to the general assembly, to the National Assembly, at its request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave. With your leave I believe that perhaps we could see this article in the law to make a clear distinction between what is written in the law and what my learned friend is implying that is the expert's personal experience and his personal position. If we have an opportunity to look at the wording of that article of the law, I'm sure that everything which -- will be much clearer to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm asking the witness about assertions in the report, and I -- Mr. Petrovic is more than welcome to put the rules, the law, to the witness on re-examination, but at the moment I want to ask the witness about what he says in his report about this. If he has no personal knowledge, he will clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, apparently Ms. Marcus is not inclined to follow your suggestion, but she rightly pointed out that if you want to deal with it, Article 9, that you have an opportunity to do so on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, just one sentence, if I may. When my learned friend puts this type of questions in the future, could she then be very clear and say what part of the expert report refers to the rule and, on the other hand, what has been made a part of the report as a personal experience? And that will make things easier and we will then be able to shed more light on the matter during re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I put -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I put to the witness the exact part that I was quoting. It's paragraph 175. I quoted the whole paragraph. It's verbatim what the witness says, and it's a question about what the witness said and the assertion which -- in which, I submit, it is entirely unclear whether his words, which also included, are based on what the rule says or what he knows to be true, and I'm going to ask him in my questions whether he can clarify what comes from the rule and what comes from other information he has. He's already answered that, and my next question will delve into that more. I'm sure that it will be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you've heard our discussion. You do not have any direct information about whether these provisions were actually enforced and observed. You just know that the rules provided for such. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, who would have had the final decision as to what information from within the service would have been included in these reports?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If the president of the republic or the National Assembly found the information to be lacking in the report provided by the minister of the interior, did they have the authority to instruct the head of the DB to provide additional information?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure if we understand each other. I -- I'm -- I believe that we have some terminology issues. When it comes to reporting, we're talking about periodical reporting every six months or every year, and those reports provided information to the superior bodies about the work of the service. This is a lengthy report that was usually sent to the National Assembly, and it was reviewed by one of the committees of the National Assembly. I believe that -- or perhaps you're talking about some interim reports, some reports that were not regular. And this is Article 9, the meaning of Article 9, that the ministry is duty-bound to report to the National Assembly, and within that report the DB service provides input, and all that is merged within one report. And it was a matter of routine. I don't think that any of those reports called for additional information. It was a matter of routine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've listened very carefully to your response, and I don't -- I still don't see what was wrong with my question. The -- I understand that they were periodical reports. I understand that it was routine. My question was about -- was: If the president of the republic or the National Assembly found the information to be lacking, did they have the authority to instruct the head of the DB to provide additional information? That was my question. I don't see why that doesn't have an answer.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this concerns certain information, but they could have acted in this way but through the minister of the interior. If they weren't happy with the report, they could have asked for it to be supplemented or for certain parts of the part [as interpreted] to be elaborated on, but this would be done through the person submitting the report. They could have made such specific requests. For example, the assembly committee could have acted in this way. So this was possible, but it had to be done through the subject submitting the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you state in paragraph 296 of your report: "The means and methods envisaged by the rules on the work of the State Security Service brought by the federal secretary of the interior on 6 July, 1990, pursuant to the powers vested in him by Article 23, paragraph 2, of the Law on the Principles of the State Security System, were applied in the work of the State Security Service of the RSUP of SR Serbia, the state security department of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, in the 1991 to 1995 period." In the next eight paragraphs, you continue to describe the application of the SDB operative and surveillance means and methods, continually citing to these rules on the work of the State Security Service. Your source in the footnote refers to D239. In paragraph 296, which I just quoted to you, you state that these rules on the work of the State Security Service were applied in the work of the DB in the 1991 to 1995 period. Now, in paragraphs 303 and 304, you then describe the role of the federal secretary of the interior with respect to the means and methods of operative application of the SDB operative and surveillance means and methods. At the end of paragraph 304, you then say that after the DB of the federal MUP "stopped functioning in October of 1992, the aforementioned powers of the federal secretary of the interior were no longer applied." Now my question is: Who was the one who carried out these functions you describe in paragraph 304 after the federal secretary of the interior stopped functioning?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously it was the republican secretariat for internal affairs. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On what do you base your opinion?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter of logic and of drawing analogies. The federal secretary is, in fact, the federal minister. When the republican ministry was responsible, well, the logical thing would be for the republican ministry to perform such duties. What's at stake here is the adoption of certain rules. Nothing specific or concrete is at stake here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But it's still not clear to me which rules applied. You said "the aforementioned powers of the federal secretary of the interior, although not repealed, were no longer applied." So this appears to me to be a situation where the standing rules in practice were not applied; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer your question. I think the report provides a clear answer. The rules on work that were adopted at the federal level were applied, so all the republics and regions applied them. But the other republics and regions, or at least some of the them at the time, had already created their own state. So the rules were in fact only applied in Serbia and in Montenegro. State security rules weren't applied at the federal level anymore. I testified to that effect in detail yesterday. I don't know whether it's necessary to go into it again. If your question was whether the text of the rules doesn't correspond to what was done, well, in my opinion, because I have no experience of the matter, well, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you correctly, although your report says that the rules, although not repealed, were no longer applied, in fact what your evidence is is that they were applied but differently. Not at the federal level anymore, but only at the republican level. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see what time it is, and I'm about to broach a different subject. If this would be a good time for the break, I could do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I would like to seek one clarification. I do understand a federal institution to work on behalf of the federal state, that is, serving the interests also of those republics forming that federal institution. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By definition, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you tell us that the malfunctioning federal institution more or less was adopted, or at least became part of the Serbian republican state security institutions. Is that correctly understood? People came to work, did their job, but not on the federal level anymore but now for the -- at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time there was no federal level anymore. Those institutions were formed as if all the republics and regions participated in them, as if they had the will to remain within that state and do everything for the benefit of territorial sovereignty and the integrity of that state, but in reality the situation on the ground was quite different. It was necessary for someone to take over these functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is: What about Montenegro at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Federal level duties in Montenegro were carried out by the security service of the Republic of Montenegro at the time. They took over all the duties that concerned their territory, and this was done within the borders that they considered to be their own. This knowledge I gained on the basis of the literature that I consulted, but I wasn't part of the leadership, so I do not know what sort of matters they discussed at meetings and for -- and so on and so forth. All these matters were legalised when the Law on the Common State of Serbia and Montenegro was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us whether the Montenegro state security system also had the benefit of having part of the premises, part of the staff, now working for their republican state security services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is nothing I can tell you about that matter in relation to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break, and we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You are an experienced academic and you have both direct professional experience as well as extensive academic knowledge of the MUP. You've served as a trainer and teacher and educator for many years. There is no doubt that many of your students look up to you. Isn't it a fact that as part of the work of a professor you must ensure not only accuracy in the work of your students, in terms of conclusions and analysis, but also accuracy in terms of citations to sources?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. One always strives to follow such rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you review a research paper prepared by a student, you would verify the accuracy of their assertions; isn't that right? What I mean is in terms of citing to the source material upon which they have based their analysis. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If you were to find, say, approximately 10 errors in one research paper where the student either incorrectly cited the source material or where the student made an assertion which could only be reasonably based upon source material but did not cite the source, you would find that research paper to not meet the standards you would expect as a professor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, one should determine the nature of the mistakes made. Perhaps the student had a different understanding of the method of referencing work, so perhaps there was a problem in the methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I intervene. Ms. Marcus, before we start a long debate and long question and answers about what you would expect students to do, I take it that you want to point at inaccuracies in sourcing. Why not directly go to that so that we do not first have an academic debate on whether it would be the students in the 2nd grade which should do better than the ones in the 1st grade and whether the other department who used them -- who would teach them how to use sources was deficient in its functioning. Let's get to the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's my next question. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 6487.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have compiled a spreadsheet, you will see before you in a moment, of unsourced assertions we have found in your report. I will provide a hard copy of this document for you to consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With leave of the Chamber, I have copies in both B/C/S and English. Perhaps the Court Usher could hand it to the witness and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: While you look at this, I would like to emphasize that where we were able to decipher what source you most likely meant to refer to, we did not include that in here. These are assertions where we truly were not able, with what I consider to be due diligence, to determine what the source was for an assertion that you made. Now, as you will see when you look through it, in our view there are 136 unsourced assertions in your report, again using the criterion that I just set out for you. So where you do not provide a source for an assertion in your report, are you basing that assertion on your own personal experience or on your expertise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I'm not sure where my learned friend is going. If she expects the professor to look at a document that contains 136 statements that aren't sourced, and if she thinks he can provide any answers about such a list, I don't think this is possible. It's a -- not possible to analyse 136 statements that have been sourced. He should be given -- the professor should be given a few days to have a look at the list and then to say whether or not there's a source for what has been listed here. I don't think proceeding in this manner at this point in time is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully intend to give the witness the opportunity to study this. Based on my estimate that I gave and which I think will be accurate, I do believe I will have to continue, at least briefly, next week. So I have no problem with him considering that. I only have a question for him about if there are unsourced assertions, are we to take it that it's based on a source or is it based on his expertise or personal experience? That's a general question about any unsourced assertions which might be found in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I deny the objection. But I'll carefully monitor that Ms. Marcus is really staying on the general level; that is, if no source is mentioned in the report, does that mean that you have not specifically used a source for that assertion. Now, the other question, whether he relies on his expertise. Of course, expertise relies often to sources which you've seen in the past but not specifically used when you drew up the report. So the witness will then have an opportunity, I take it, to add anything to the answer to the very general question by giving further details on any specific matter contained in this -- in this spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have heard my comments and my decision on the objection, Mr. Milosevic. At this moment we -- Ms. Marcus is asking you a rather general question. If you could briefly answer that question and then you'll have a further opportunity to -- to further choose your position in -- on any specific matter in this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I only have two general questions for you on the matter of unsourced assertion, generally. So to ask you again the one that I asked before: In cases where you do not provide a source for an assertion in your report, are you basing that assertion on your own personal experience or on your expertise in terms of your research and training?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say without having a look at each individual assertion, but in general I didn't think it was necessary to provide sources for all the assertions made because I took it for granted -- or we take for granted that I'm an expert and that on the basis of my expertise I can form certain opinions. So I used my scientific knowledge in a general sense, if that's what you're asking me about. But I would have to look at each individual assertion to be able to answer your question. I'm not sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That does answer my question as well as my other question. Before we leave this with you for now, I'll just make mention: Because of the timing on when we prepared this, there are some comments in there regarding translations. You are free to ignore those. Those are about an administrative consideration. We need English translations for the materials. So to the extent any comment in there accidentally is included that relates to translations, please -- please just ignore that. The focus for this issue is on the lack of sourcing, and it'll be clear from the entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I'm done with this document at the moment, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that you wish that the witness keeps his copy so that he ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would keep your copy. And, well, the practical way of dealing with it, if the witness goes through it, Ms. Marcus, I don't expect you that he gives all his specific answers in every single detail here in court when giving testimony, or would you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's fair for him to have a chance to comment on it, but I did not intend for the witness no note one by one what the sources were. In fact, from my point of view his answer is clear. What he gave just now is the answer that I was looking -- the information I was seeking. Now, it is fair only for him to have an opportunity to respond, but I certainly don't -- wouldn't ask him item by item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what we are seeking -- but perhaps, Mr. Petrovic, I first give you an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that this is an impossible mission or a failure to understand the nature of an expert report. Have a look at item 1, Your Honour, which relates to paragraph 99. Here it says the responsibility of the department is defined in detail in the documents on internal organisation. You have at least 15 pages in this report that deal with this issue, at least 15 pages, and my learned friend puts a question about the source. She must have read the report and she can see that there are at least 15 pages in the report that go into the details of these documents on organisation. So I really do not understand what is expected of this expert witness. I do apologise, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to -- to intervene for a second. It may be a very clear example. The expert has given his answer to the general questions. If, for example, number 1 and a few other items would receive an answer like, "I have not detailed the source here, but in many other paragraphs I gave the detailed sources when I went to the details of this observation," then that is a comment on the question and the general answer given. I can imagine that for number 25 - I have not looked at it - that he says, "You're right, I've forgotten to mention the source which I specifically have but failed to put in the footnote." Or on another matter, to say, "Well, in general, numbers 2, 15, 17, 21, they are mainly based on my experience in the service rather than on academic sources or legal texts which I specifically used to make that assertion." That is the kind of comment we would allow the witness to give to the extent that he thinks this it's fair in addition to his answer to the general questions that would be fair for him to give. Is that, Ms. Marcus, approximately what you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Your Honour. We have endeavoured to focus on those where we couldn't really determine, but that doesn't exclude the possibility, that there may be some in there that are easily explicable. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Either by reference to other parts of the report. And we do not expect the witness to go through that in detail, but to give him a fair opportunity to respond to what seems to be a question of not being very accurate, even as suggested, but I stopped at worse as a student. Let's just focus on what the witness would like to say without going into every single detail of the list, but, rather, in similar general terms to say, 20 per cent of it I've forgotten to give the source. Such kind of remarks. And, Ms. Marcus, would you agree with me that such comments could be given in -- if the witness would prefer to write them down, that that may be okay, but that otherwise some comments on your list could be given in some ten to 12 minutes, is that ... I'm trying to manage this trial as well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would say maximum. But yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Milosevic, I saw you raising your hand. Yes, you may address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but obviously either I don't understand the Prosecution or the Prosecution doesn't understand what is written here. Well, if one casts just a brief glance at this first page, last item, that concerns paragraph 127, it says the author referred to such and such an article, 93, item 2, if that's the one. But he says -- but it says he didn't provide it -- a source. In footnote 167, however, a source is referred to. On the rules on job specification --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down when reading out parts of the text as it's impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down, because it's a common experience that once you -- once you start reading, that you usually start speaking more quickly as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the information provided in the footnotes, the notes that were made and that relate to this specific example we're discussing, well, we can see that in Article 127, in brackets. The decree on the professions of authorised officials of the organs of internal affairs and on the professions of the republican secretariat for internal affairs, published in the official bulletin of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, number 58, in 1989. I can't see anything missing here. So I said that things could be quoted in various ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I may just briefly inquire into that. What is different in paragraph 127 is that the sources are not in the footnotes but in the text themselves. Now, I haven't seen the list of sources. Now, does that include the sources which are contained in the text, or would it be just the sources in the footnotes, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, some documents are mentioned in several places. Therefore, they will be found in footnotes in the places where it is most logical for them to be found. For example, the 2D941, the decree on jobs and positions, is in paragraph 358, footnote 346. In the part that is directly concerned with that decree where that decree is the main topic, there is a source there, and, again, the indication of the document, the Official Gazette, and the 2D number, obviously. Paragraphs are 358, 359, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the issue is perhaps not primarily that it's not sourced, because paragraph 127 gives sources, but whether that source is available to the Prosecution and in such a way that it also is able to locate where to find it, that source. Ms. Marcus, is that part of the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That would be part of the problem, Your Honour. That doesn't -- in other words, this list includes sources which were not provided and therefore we couldn't verify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- as well as where a source for an assertion was not provided at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have to look at it either -- but that might be more a problem for Mr. Petrovic than it is for Mr. Milosevic, that to the extent source material is not yet in evidence and is not provided in a way so that Ms. Marcus can locate it, then there may be a problem. Of course, the Chamber has the same problem, because what is in evidence we can look at, but when reading the report, not even having lists of supporting material, let alone that we have seen them all and that they are in evidence, that creates a procedural problem, Mr. Petrovic, for which you -- we cannot blame Ms. Marcus at this moment. But apparently there are also other matters in the list that are assertions where the problem is not where to find the source or whether the source is available because a reference to that source exists, but a reference is not yet the source itself. But the other category is assertions which are without sources at all, and that was, I think, one of the main subjects of the question put by Ms. Marcus to the witness a minute ago. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just would like to add one brief point. There were a number of people who worked very, very hard on this. This list is under-inclusive, if anything. Where we could determine through reasonable investigations which, if there was a cross-referencing issue, was very difficult to do, we -- I did not include that here, so we had a much more extensive list. And then for those which we could determine with our own investigations, we -- we tried really not to include them. So I -- as I say this, there may be something in here which is just simply because we could not determine what the source was. We -- as far -- to the best of our knowledge, we simply couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, therefore, we -- giving this list to the witness, wouldn't it be fair to ask him to primarily focus not on matters he sourced but where the source may not be available to you? So I think the one paragraph 127 seems to be clear in that respect and doesn't need any further comment, not to even deal with matters of translation but to focus mainly on those items where the Prosecution alleges that no source is given at all, and then not to go through them one by one but to read them, to consider them, and to see whether there is a kind of an answer to those assertions by the Prosecution. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave. Everybody who's benevolent can see what the whole thing is all about. Look at 358, look at footnote that accompanies that paragraph, and look at 127. I simply cannot believe that there is somebody who cannot collate these two things and cannot understand what we're talking about. I'm sorry for being a bit aggressive, but a lot of effort has been invested in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petrovic, perhaps I should be the last at this moment to not forgive you some small eruption of emotion. Yesterday I didn't always use the most gentle words when I -- we were discussing the matter of the levels above Mr. Simatovic. Although my colleagues agreed with the content of my remarks, I also noted that they certainly would have used a more gentle tone, and I take that as guidance for the future. So I'm not blaming you for being a bit upset about the matter, but we are not going to spend time on this discussion in court. I would suggest that you try to resolve this matter with Ms. Marcus in such a way that you assist her and say, "Well, we have difficulties in understanding why you couldn't resolve this or this or this," and then to try to find common ground for that and to see what really is important to know more about, perhaps strike a few items. Try to see how far you could come. And then if that does not resolve the matter, if you could not come to an agreement on that, rather than spending time on it in court in the way we just started to do that, I would invite you to meet with me at 7.00 in the morning to further discuss the practical approach of this matter. Perhaps, in view of circumstances, that I would delay it until 8.00 or that Ms. Marcus, apparently relying on the work of some others, would seek assistance or even replacements by those who worked hard on this. And then I'm almost certain that we would have resolved most of it by 9.00 and then we could spend our time in court again on what we're here for, that is, to hear evidence. Ms. Marcus, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The section of your report which deals with the position of Franko Simatovic, that is, section 8 of your report - it contains 39 paragraphs - it is entirely based upon his personnel file and the applicable DB rules and regulations. You state that you did view some personnel files and other decisions, as we discussed earlier, but you don't cite to them. You make the following assertions in the Franko Simatovic section which, the way they are worded, suggest that you do have or did obtain some concrete information about Mr. Simatovic's actual activities. You say in paragraph 338, for example, that Mr. Simatovic discharged certain duties. You use that same term in paragraphs 356 and 364. I would like to focus now on your assertion in paragraph 336 and ask you some questions about that. In paragraph 336, you describe Frenki's purported assignment to Kosovo from the 12th of April, 1991, to 17th of October, 1991. You state: "From 12 April 1991 to 17 October 1991, Franko Simatovic was assigned for a stint of duty to the State Security Service of the provincial secretariat of the interior of AP Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P2403. I'm not sure if this is under seal. Perhaps I could ask the -- it is? Okay, and not broadcast it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you also mention Mr. Simatovic's alleged deployment to Kosovo in footnote 335, which is a footnote to paragraph 348. This assertion is based purely upon the document in Mr. Simatovic's personnel file which describes his deployment to Kosovo, which you cite as P2403 and which is on our screens; is that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please be more specific and tell me what you want me to say? Maybe the interpretation was not good. What am I supposed to answer? Is this the document or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me intervene here. Listen carefully, Mr. Milosevic, to what Ms. Marcus asked you. The question was whether the assertion you made in the report was based purely upon the document we see in front of us. So that this -- was this your one and only source, or was there any other source for your assertion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, this is the decision by which he was dispatched. There is another document showing that a few individuals were deployed at the same time. In this case, in a decision on deployment it has to say that somebody is deployed. I really don't know what's in dispute. I didn't accompany him personally to Kosovo to see whether he really went there. I base my assertions on this public document, and that public document is true unless proven not true. It says very clearly here from the 12th to -- the date is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your answer apparently is: "I based my assertion on this document and also on the fact that I've seen similar documents for other persons." Your comment on whether the public document is true unless proven not to be true is, first of all, for this Chamber and, second, is more complex than you present it. Because the document may be true in the sense of authentic; the document may be true in the sense of that it was produced on the date it gives; the document may be, for example, not true on whether what was written down as a decision or an order was executed after that. So the truth of a document is a complex matter. I don't have to explain that to you as a specialist in criminal law and procedure, and there is no need to further discuss that because we'll have to do that circle. Therefore, it's this document that you rely upon and you add to that that you have seen similar documents, apparently, of persons who were assigned to similar tasks in the same period of time. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 336, where you cite this document, you do not discuss anything specific about this document. You do not note, for example, that this document, which is your source regarding Frenki's alleged deployment to Kosovo, is dated the 18th of March, 1992; thus, this was a retroactive deployment. You do not mention that Frenki's retroactive deployment to Kosovo was signed by Jovica Stanisic, the first accused. You are aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I kindly ask you to look at footnote 320 where it says clearly that the document was issued on the 18th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may be true. The report, although giving the information, does not point at retroactivity, and I think that's mainly what Ms. Marcus is talking about. Ms. Marcus, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you've told us that you've seen the indictment, you are aware that both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic have been charged with crimes allegedly comitted in Croatia in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can understand, they are charged with participating in a joint criminal enterprise. However, I -- I did not ponder the whole thing. I was just curious and that's why I read it, but I didn't delve too much into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: But you did know that the issue of Mr. Simatovic's whereabouts in 1991 is a critical issue to this case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are implying here. But whatever you are trying to imply, it doesn't really hold water. I based my assertions on the document. I said when it was issued. I didn't go into any other detail because I'm not aware of them. I can't testify about something that I don't know and that I didn't see. I can only testify about this document. I told you, and I stated when it was issued, and everybody can see that. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question simply was whether you did know that the issue of Mr. Simatovic's whereabouts in 1991 is a critical issue to this case. That's the question. Now, either you knew, then you answer by "yes," or you didn't know, then you answer by "no." That's the issue. It's not the start of a debate between you and Ms. Marcus. Please proceed. And please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. I read the indictment only after I had written my report. It was only then that I actually saw it, and it could not have affected my work on the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you not find the retroactive nature of the deployment to be significant to discuss in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have already answered that by stating the precise date when this document was issued. You will see that clearly stated in the footnote. I didn't consider that I should do anything else. When I analysed his career and his moves in the career, I used documents. And that's what I did. I did not think that I had to do a complete reconstruction of his tours at every moment. And as to your question, I believe that I have answered your question already by citing the document and the date when it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier some other documents that you also say that you consulted in reaching the assertion that you reach here. Can you tell us what those other documents are? The way you referred to them is, "There is --" oh, it's one document. I apologise. What you said was: "There is another document showing that a few individuals were deployed at the same time." Is that another document in Mr. Simatovic's personnel file or is that yet another document that you consulted?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was a document in which the minister of the interior deployed a certain number of individuals to Kosovo. I'm not sure whether it was at that moment that -- but that was common practice, for people to be deployed based on such decision -- decisions. The minister issued a decision, and then each employee who was deployed would be issued with their individual deployment decision. I'm talking about what common practice was. First there was a decision, and based on that decision individual decisions would be issued and filed in each of the individuals' personnel files.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was it common practice for these deployments to be issued retroactively?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you saw that the date of the deployment post-dated the date -- the alleged date -- sorry, the date of this decision on deployment post-dated the alleged date of deployment, did you not think to ask the Simatovic Defence whether they had any additional documentation, or simply, in your researcher's mind, did you not query the retroactive nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not want to delve on that because I thought it would be tantamount to dealing with facts, and I thought that what I pointed out would suffice, because it looked very non-ambiguous to me, so I did not go into the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There are in evidence, in fact, at least three other retroactive deployments of DB members to Kosovo, all dated March 1992, all pertaining to purported deployments to Kosovo in 1991, all signed by Jovica Stanisic, all contained in DB personnel files for these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer the Chamber to P2723; P474, page 6 in English and 45 in B/C/S; and P3012.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There are also in evidence three other retroactive deployments on documents dated late 1995, all for retroactive deployment to Sremska Mitrovica in -- earlier in 1995, one signed by Jovica Stanisic and two signed by Milan Prodanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your reference, that is P474, page 17 in English and 54 in B/C/S; P548; and P2755.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in the case of all six of these purported retroactive deployments, there has been evidence in this case that during these -- the time-period of these deployments to Kosovo and Sremska Mitrovica, these individuals were actually operating as part of the DB in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer the Chamber to the following: The transcript of the 1st of September, 2011, at pages 13749 to 13782; to the transcript of the 2nd of February, 2012, at transcript pages 16909 to 16911; the transcript of 31 January, 2012, at page 16707 to 16708. I refer you to P537. And, finally, P466, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry for that list of references. Here's my question: In this document that you see in front of you, P2403, under what legal provisions would it have been possible -- let me change the introduction to my question. Under what legal provisions would it have been possible to deploy DB members to Croatia in 1991 and Bosnia in 1995 to engage in joint combat operations with other Serb forces in those areas?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question because I really don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't know what rules would have provided for that, or the rules did not provide for that?
