utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what the legal foundation for that was. I really don't know. I -- personally, I don't know whether there was a legal foundation and what it was. Unless we go back to what we said yesterday, and that was that there was a legal foundation. That was discussed yesterday. But if you want me to answer your question more specifically by citing a law or an article there, I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I thank the Chamber again for the permission to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you're not able to answer the question of whether it would have been possible, legally, for the DB to officially deploy individuals to Croatia in 1991 and Bosnia in 1995 to participate in joint combat operations; do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question if you're asking me to refer to the exact article. We spoke about a constitutional basis, a legal basis for co-operation, yesterday, but I can't tell you exactly which article of the rules is concerned. I don't know what to say. Yesterday I explained in detail that there were -- there was a constitutional and legal basis for combat operations in particular. I really don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your very last comment. You said that yesterday you explained in detail that there was a constitutional and legal basis for combat operations. Does that mean that you know that there was a legal basis for these deployments by the DB to Croatia in 1991 and Bosnia in 1995 but you just can't cite the article for us, or you don't know whether it was possible, legally, to carry out those deployments for the purposes of joint combat operations?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they could be involved in intelligence operations. I'm only speaking about the intelligence component within the service, not the combat component. So I don't know where this terminology comes from. I never mentioned combat operations yesterday. I only mentioned intelligence and security tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I may analyse, what happens at this moment is the following. Ms. Marcus asks you whether there was a legal basis for DB members to be sent abroad to participate, and she gave the places that the -- the republics and the time-period. Whether there was a legal basis for them to be sent to participate in combat operations. Your first answer was, I wouldn't know exactly what legal provision would provide for that. Then you refer to what you said yesterday, and from what I remember from yesterday is that you pointed at certain provisions which would allow for intelligence activity both within the state borders and outside the state borders. And then you say, But I never used the word "combat." I think that's accurate. Therefore, apparently the crux of the matter is where Ms. Marcus asks you whether there would be a basis for sending DB members for combat operations, that what you said yesterday, apparently, does not apply. That's at least how I understood your last observation, that you never used the word "combat." So we are back, more or less, at square one. What you said yesterday, if I understand you well, is not an answer to the question of Ms. Marcus and whether any provision exists which would allow for DB members to be sent abroad in that period of time to the places mentioned, you just say, I -- I do not know of the existence of such a legal provision, which is -- does not mean that it does not exist but at least that it does not come to your mind at this moment. Is this analysis of a rather confusing question and answer situation, is that analysis accurate as far as you are concerned, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it also accurate as far as you are concerned, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that if the DB were deploying individuals to Croatia and Bosnia in 1991 and 1995 to participate in joint combat operations they would have had to create documents to conceal this deployment in order to fit into the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is that it's possible to put leading questions in the course of cross-examination. I do understand that. I can't confirm that anyone created documents of any kind to cover anything up. I don't know what the Prosecution is getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that wasn't the question. The question was that if it would be true that DB were deploying individuals to Croatia and Bosnia in 1991 and 1995 to participate in joint combat, that you would have to create documents to conceal that this happened because it would not fit into the rules and the regulations, so therefore you could not put on paper what actually happened. That is a different question from whether such documents were produced to conceal. It's a more or less theoretical question. Could you answer it? If you can, please do so. If you say, I can't answer it, then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the legal basis is concerned, I said I knew nothing about such a basis. But as you, yourself, said, Your Honour, that doesn't mean that there is no such basis. All it means is that I can't remember anything about it now. As far as covering up things, I really don't think that there was the need to act in that way. If everything was done in compliance with the rules of service, in accordance with the rules of service there would not have been any reason to try and conceal anything. So I really cannot say whether there were such cases or not, and I don't even know how I would answer that question in a purely theoretical way. It would be more logical not to create documents of any kind apart from documents that could subsequently prove to be compromising, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P979.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, what you will see in a moment is an order signed by Frenki, dated the 16th of June, 1991, in Golubic, RSK, ordering weapons and armament to be removed from the fortress to Golubic. What rules would have permitted Frenki's involvement in the movement of weapons in Croatia and Golubic in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two comments: The witness is not a factual witness. And my second comment concerns this document which is presented as if one had determined that this was Frenki's signature. This is in dispute. It would be fair to tell the witness what the status of this document is. This is an exhibit, but it is an exhibit that is contested by one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, since Ms. Marcus did not ask for facts, she could also have easily left out the question as to who signed it, because it's a matter of whether you can issue such decisions yes or no, whether it was by Mr. Simatovic or by anyone else, isn't it? Because we're talking about the rules and what was permitted under the rules. To that extent, I think, Ms. Marcus, you're not asking for facts but rather whether there would be a legal basis for a decision like this where the Prosecution believes that it was signed by Mr. Simatovic. But even if that would not be true, still the question remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. However, and perhaps it was the faulty language in my question, I did want to know -- I am focussing on this section of the report on Mr. Simatovic. I did want to know which positions the rules governing the positions that have been set out by the witness would have permitted his involve -- Mr. Simatovic's involvement in the activities in here. But it is true I did not mention that it -- that it is -- the signature is contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are asking what rule would allow a person in the position of Mr. Simatovic, leaving apart whether he was the one who assigned this or not, but which rule would allow for this activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- the documents that the witness studied in Mr. Simatovic's file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Knowing what his position was. Could you answer that question. So don't bother about whether the signature is the one of Mr. Simatovic or not, but you may answer the question on an assumption that the document was signed by a person in a position like the one you knew at the time was held by Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the authenticity of the document is contested because in the heading it says "The Republic of Serbia, the SAO Krajina," and so on and so forth. So I have doubts about its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The authenticity we'll discuss elsewhere. I would invite you to answer the question that was put to you by Ms. Marcus and which I rephrased. What rule would allow a person in the position of Mr. Simatovic which would -- rule would allow for the activity as described in this document? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the rules of service, he could go abroad and be involved in intelligence work there. That's what I can say in general terms. He could have done everything in accordance with those rules. But there's nothing I can say about this particular case. This document, I've never seen it before. But as I have said, it is odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Could I then ask you, because you are again not answering the question, because I referred to the activity described in this document. Then a simple question is: Is an order to have weapons and armament to be retreated from the fortress to Golubic, is that intelligence activity or is that anything else? Or let's say if it's not intelligence, to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document doesn't show that the activity concerned was a matter for intelligence. So if we interpret the language of this document, I'd say that isn't the case. It's obvious that other activities are at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, therefore, you would agree with me that you have not answered the question, because the question was: What is the legal basis for the activity described in this document for a person in the position of Mr. Simatovic? Your answer was that Mr. Simatovic could have done other things abroad, that is, intelligence, but the question was: What is the legal basis for these activities described in this document for a person in the position of Mr. Simatovic? Could you answer that question. First, perhaps, does a legal basis for this kind of activity, does that exist; and if so, where is it to be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we exclude the usual constitutional and legally basis, well, I don't know on the basis of what sort of documents that this could be done. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up P1121 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. May we have a break, Your Honours, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, Ms. Marcus, and we'll resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Is this P1121 that we see on our screens? Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, this is a report dated the 19th of July, 1991, Mr. Milosevic, regarding TO and MUP combat operations in the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the areas of Benkovac and Obrovac. The report states that it's copied to Frenki. What would have been the MUP regulations which would have provided that Frenki is to be copied on such reports in July 1991 during the time he was purportedly deployed to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we have the same case. Again, I really am not an expert for these issues. I can't answer such a question. The SDB of the Republic of Serbia didn't draft this document, so I really can't comment on it. You can see that those who authored the document are not from that body, and I know nothing about the facts that relate to this case, so I can't say anything. All I can say is that this is not a report from the SDB or, rather, the RDB. Given the layout, that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I didn't ask you about the document. I asked you about the MUP regulations. That is your expertise - MUP regulations and rules and laws. In all my questions, I've been asking -- not all, but in most of my questions, that's the point I'm trying to ask you about. You've told us, according the documents you've consulted, what Frenki's position was. You've told us about what the rules and regulations would have said about what tasks and responsibilities he would have carried out pursuant to those rules. Now, my question specifically was which MUP regulations or rules or laws would have provided for Frenki to be copied on reports in July 1991 during the time that he was purportedly deployed to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I said. I just don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Then let me just clarify with one last follow-up question on this. Isn't it a fact that you do not know of my MUP regulations which would have provided for Mr. Simatovic to have been copied on documents such as this in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I haven't quite understood that question. Perhaps the interpretation was not quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps I spoke too quickly and the interpreters couldn't follow me. I apologise if that was the case. Let me repeat my last question. Isn't it a fact that you do not know of any MUP regulations which would have provided for Mr. Simatovic to have been copied on documents such as this in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not saying that there were no such rules or that there are no such rules. All I'm saying is that I'm not aware of any such rules, so I can't provide you with a precise explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I move on, I'd just like to refer the Chamber also to Exhibit P1122. I am finished with this document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wonder what precisely my learned friend is doing. First of all, this witness hasn't asserted that there was a regulation. Secondly, the witness - quite fairly, in my submission - said, well, this document doesn't come from the Ministry of the Interior, so why would there, effectively, be a rule? If I, for example, send the Prosecution a document, one wouldn't expect the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I must say that what you're saying now came to my mind as well. I sometimes receive mail without any rule providing for me receiving that mail. Nevertheless, it becomes argumentive. And to be quite honest, Ms. Marcus also when she lists a long series of sources which give a different -- sheds a different light on the events which is the subject of the examination, then, of course, no one could reasonably expect at that moment the Chamber to verify all that. And, as a matter of fact, I think it's already summarising what the evidence is, which is, during the testimony of a witness, not strictly necessary and should perhaps even be avoided, and then later in final briefs or at any other moment you could put that all in the right context. Ms. Marcus, if there's one specific document you think it would assist us to look at when hearing this evidence, yes, of course, that would help, but to receive seven, eight, or nine sources with all the numbers, I could not even have them on my screen at the same time. Let's try to -- the point you're apparently seeking to make, Ms. Marcus, is that for some activities, including some of the accused, for which evidence has been presented, that you would, through this witness, want to establish that there was no legal basis for that. If that is the point you intended to make, I think whether we accept it or not is another matter, but you have, I would say -- what you wanted to establish is perfectly clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was, indeed, part of the point. I hope the rest will be clearer from the examination. Now, in terms of references, Your Honour, what I try to do is to provide the basis for my questions and put that right in the record at the point where I ask that question. There have been other times where I've put a question and the Defence has asked what the basis was for that question. So now I'm doing it. I do it as a matter of course now. And it's become something which I think could be helpful to both parties and the Chamber in terms of cross-referencing. Now, that said, if Your Honour prefers me to not do that, then I will not make those references during the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you listened well to me, I didn't say never do it, but do it within certain limits and only when it assists the Chamber at the very moment of hearing the evidence to better understand it. Now, I can imagine that if you have looked for all these sources, you might -- it might assist the other parties fairly well in preparing. So if you have a list and say, okay, this and this is it, then to prepare for re-examination, et cetera, might be very helpful. So I'm not saying don't do these kind of things, but let's avoid that it becomes argument more, such as there is a lot of evidence that contradicts what the witness says. That's appropriately done at another moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, in the JATD section of your report you do not mention the role of Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic. Is it your evidence that Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic had nothing to the with the JATD?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what is stated quite explicitly here, what is written quite explicitly here. I don't know what else I could say. I didn't say that they were aware of anything else. I don't really know what your question is about. Jovica Stanisic didn't establish the JATD. It was based -- it was formed on the basis of the Law on Internal Affairs, as you can see here, by the minister of the interior, Zoran Sokolovic. So I don't understand where I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- sorry to interrupt you. I simply asked you about what was not there and whether it was intentionally not there. So you did not mention the roles of the accused in the JATD. My question was simply: Is it your evidence, therefore, that Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic had nothing to do with the JATD, and that's why you didn't make mention of them in that section?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for which I didn't mention that is that here it says quite explicitly who formed the unit and when. It states who was in command of the unit, and you can see who the deputy commander was and where the centre was located. The individuals that you have asked me about are not mentioned in the documents that I examined. None of them was a commander or assistant. So I don't see why I should mention this, given the manner in which I compiled my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again, you are going around the question. You say, well, they were not commanders, et cetera. The simple question was: Did you not mention Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic because on the basis of the material you went through that you did not find any link, any personal link, of one of the two or both with the JATD? And I take it, Ms. Marcus, that you did not include the mere fact that they were working in the same state organ but whether there was any personal dealing by Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic with the JATD.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How I prepared this part and the materials that I had at my disposal in a way led me to write what I did. I just enumerated those individuals in various positions based on documents. I repeat once again, and I regret that I have to repeat over and over again, that I am not a fact witness and I don't know what the roles of all the individuals were. I only know what has been confirmed officially by documents. I'm talking about people's position and jobs. Of course chief of service was well aware of activities, but it is only my assumption. I cannot confirm that for a fact, because there's no document relating these individuals to any of the places that are mentioned in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, the simple answer to my question would be "no," because on the basis of the material you went through, you did not find any link, any personal link or any personal dealing with -- of Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Stanisic with the JATD. A simple "no" would have answered my question, I think, unless I misunderstood your question -- your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood me well. You can't tell that based on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which leaves another question. If you would have any personal knowledge, then, of course, although you were called here as an expert and you are writing a report, then I would put the question to you as well whether you have any knowledge outside of your expertise, and this would then not be a clarification of your report but seeking evidence from you to the extent you know any facts about Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic in a link with the JATD.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I saw some signatures, but I can't remember what they were. I believe that they belonged to a different administration, but I'm not sure. One signature was put on behalf of somebody else, of the deputy commander Radonjic. I believe it was Franko Simatovic who signed on his behalf. And if you remember, the Defence counsel asked me whether it would have been customary for Franko Simatovic to sign on somebody's behalf if that person was there, if the commander was there, but I can't confirm or deny. I can't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not interested in what you learned in this courtroom through the questions. I'm interested in any knowledge you may have, and you may have had before you arrived in The Hague, about any personal dealing or any personal involvement of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic with the JATD. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were certainly linked to that, but I don't know what facts we're talking about. If I were to see documents, I could provide comments on those documents. But without any documents, I don't know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes people know things even without looking at documents. What I'm asking you is about any personal knowledge you may have about that, and not whether when inspecting documents you would find something. I'm interested: Do you have any knowledge, any factual knowledge, about any dealing of one of the two accused, Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic, with the JATD? If you have it, please tell us what it is. If you don't have it, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 6488. Your Honours, what's going to come up on our screens is a demonstrative exhibit which we have prepared. I would compare it most closely to the slides, for example, that we've prepared for our 98 bis submission. It is not intended to be evidence. It is merely a tool to cross-reference evidence to assist the Chamber and the Defence. Now, there are three of them, each one containing underlying documents, and those were the documents that were in the three respective binders that the witness was asked to review. Now, I have prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have hard copies, Your Honour, for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we had two B/C/S versions earlier on our screen, and now we have a B/C/S and an English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave, I would hand out the hard copies. The electronic versions were sent to the Defence previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Please, could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Each of the packets that are handed out - there is an English version -- there's an English packet, B/C/S packets - each one contains all three charts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For Mr. Jordash an English copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, of the charts in the packet, the one that I am going to ask you to look at and which is on our screens, appears to be the third one in the packet, if they're all in the same order. It's the one containing what we say is a list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I -- I do think that I do have an objection to this. First -- I mean, obviously I don't know what the Prosecution is going to do, but what I can see in relation to these demonstrative exhibits, as they are termed, are essentially submissions. Let's take page 1 of this package. Evidence -- it's entitled "Evidence Relating to Killed Members of the Unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. We are back now to the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. "Evidence Relating to Killed Members of the Unit." First of all, it appears, on the face of it, a way of packaging the Prosecution evidence to make submissions to the Court in a way which, I submit, we've seen my learned friend doing today and we've seen her doing it before. It's a way of making submissions to Your Honours, effectively. That's the first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could we first ask Ms. Marcus what she's intending to do with it. If she wants to say, Well, I want the witness to count whether number one consists of four pages, and then establish that. Or ... I mean, I've got no idea what Ms. Marcus is intending to do. It -- although I can imagine that one thinks of going into facts where the witness until now has clearly stated that he has no knowledge of any facts. And I would not expect him, but of course it would be for the witness to say -- would be for the witness to say that he would have knowledge of these kind of fact where he has shown earlier not to have of many, many factual activities. Ms. Marcus, what is it that you would like to do with this material?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Now, what -- what Mr. Jordash says is partially accurate, and we would be happy -- I would be happy later, if the Chamber prefers, to tender this through a submission. At this point what it's meant to do was to organise material for the witness to consider. The questions that I will ask the witness will pertain to selections of documents that are noted on these charts. I will ask him questions directly pertaining to his expertise and the rules and regulations. I will, of course, ask him if the documentary evidence that he has consulted might change his opinion. And I will -- and this is, essentially, putting our case very clearly to the witness and rebutting the assertions that he makes in his report. Now, in terms of the quantity of materials underlying these charts, I'm in the Chamber's hands. Some of it is to assist -- it's presented in this way to assist to present our case very clearly as to what documentary evidence is linked to what other documentary evidence. It is, in fact, a representation of a piece of our case. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I've done it in this context because these are the materials that we've provided to the witness and he can also have an opportunity to understand how that -- those documents that we showed to him, how they fit into our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness is not here to learn about the Prosecution's case. The witness is here to give evidence. And until now, one of the them -- one of the main elements of the evidence has been that the witness has presented a lot of documents on the structure, the rules, as far as Mr. Simatovic is concerned, about his positions, his appointment, et cetera, et cetera. And whenever we entered into any area where we asked him what happened, whether the reality was in accordance with the rules or not, usually the witness said that he couldn't tell us. There's not much - I'm not saying nothing - in his report about what happened in reality, but I'm -- would you just allow me to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, we have some concern about in what direction it will go. That concern has not been removed entirely by your explanation. You have five minutes to put questions to the witness in relation to whatever material is in here, and we'll stop you once you go beyond what you said you would do, that is, to elicit evidence based on the expertise of this witness. So, therefore, you are limited to that. We don't want to have a repetition of a few other things that we heard today, and we are not at this moment assisted by -- through this witness giving the Chamber an overview of elements of your case which is -- of course everything is linked to what the witness says, but we would like to avoid that to happen. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to jump up now, but I also did want to point out that -- and this is an equal concern, that listed within this document are 48 - that was my quick count - 48 pieces of fresh evidence. Sixty -- for all the 65 ter numbers are fresh evidence. It's -- this is not only, in our submission, an attempt to make a lengthy submission, but an attempt to, at the close of the case, introduce as much of the Prosecution's archives as they can possibly manage under the guise of this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hadn't noticed that, but I see that a footnote usually starts with the words "65 ter."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have been to some extent generous in this respect, to say that if the evidence of the witness triggers -- if he knows something specific which the Prosecution could not have foreseen, they could not have made that selection in advance. Until now, I do not see any part of the evidence which is mainly about rules and regulations and legislation which would trigger specific knowledge about individual cases. But, Mr. Petrovic, I had started speaking before I had given you an opportunity to add something to what Mr. Jordash said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to say this, maybe somewhat belatedly, but I hope you will allow me to say what I'm going to say. One of the reasons why my learned friend has presented this to the witness is whether the witness faced with the documents might change his opinion. She has provided 45 documents about the JATD that allegedly bear Simatovic's signature. And now if the witness is expected to form a different opinion on a set of new documents, it would only be fair that he were provided with all the documents about the same topic, but a lot of them bear different person's signatures or they are not signed at all. If he is expected to change his opinion, then he would have to be provided with a whole set of documents, not only those that were signed by or initialled by Simatovic. So he should be provided with all the rest of documents, those bearing other people's signatures or initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might even make it worse, because the change of opinion, of course, Ms. Marcus, I do not know what it is, what opinion you are talking about. But if it -- if there's any suggestion that this witness's opinion as an expert was that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were not in any way linked -- to be linked, no personal dealings with the JATD, then that is not the opinion of this witness. This witness's opinion is that, reviewing the materials he has reviewed, and that's mainly rules and regulations, that he did not find anything in those documents which would link Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic to the JATD in terms of personal dealings with that. Now, the witness did not tell us that they had no personal dealings with it. The witness said that on the basis of the inspection of the documents he did not find any such link. So if it would be your intention, by showing a lot of documents to the witness, to challenge that finding, I mean, even if he would be convinced at the very end of this -- of these documents that he would be -- say, "Well, of course; how could you think of any other thing?" that wouldn't change his opinion, because his opinion is limited to what he found when he inspected the documents. Now, to put to a witness new material and then to ask him what conclusions he would draw from that is certainly not something which falls within the scope of the expertise of this witness. You would seek -- perhaps he would know a bit more about the context, but you would seek him to draw conclusions on the basis of documentary evidence for which he is not specifically trained, it's not within his specific skills. And apart from that, it's for the Chamber to draw such conclusions on the basis of these documents. May that be of guidance when I give you five minutes to demonstrate that the only thing you are doing, including with this material, is to elicit further expert knowledge, expert evidence, from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I -- before I commence with my five minutes on that, may I please respond to what's been going on, to make a submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, what happened is we had objections in two rounds; first the general ones, and then the second one. I did not yet touch upon the fresh evidence issue. I just briefly referred to the Chamber's approach to this, but I didn't elaborate on that. If that is a matter you would want to include or if there would be anything else you would like to further say in response to Mr. Jordash and Mr. Petrovic, you may do so now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On the matter of fresh evidence, just in response to your last comment, Your Honour, we can -- we do intend to tender the underlying materials in rebuttal, and my intention was to deal with that at the end of the witness's testimony, and I will be prepared at that time, obviously, to respond to any matters relating to the admissibility of that material. I would like to respond to some other points that were raised by the Defence. This is a case about the Serbian MUP, and this is the Defence MUP expert. In fact, this is the only MUP expert to testify in this case for either party. Now, I recognise that the Defence and the expert both concede and that the Chamber acknowledges that the intention underlying this report was, perhaps, not to say what actually happened but, rather, to present what should have happened had the rules been followed. That said, Your Honour, the report the way it stands does not read as conditional. The author states as early as in his introductory remarks: The police expert report shall present a study on the functioning of organs of the interior. That's paragraph 1. Paragraph 4: Part five of the study analyses, among other things, the exercise of the managerial function of the chief of the SDB. Paragraph 6: Part seven of the study deals with the establishment and activity of the 2nd Administration. Paragraph 8: Part nine of the study - which is the JATD section - pursuant to the legal documents related to the JATD, issues are discussed including the relationship between active and reserve members, the manner of recruitment and engagement, the rights and obligations of numbers, and the pay for engaging the reserve force in the field. And finally, and most prominently, paragraph 9 of the introduction: This methodological approach in the expert report, based on the relevant documents, makes it possible to ascertain in detail the place and role of Franko Simatovic in the functioning of the SDB of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia; i.e., the duties that he de facto and de jure discharged in the period from 1991 to 1995. Now, if the Defence acknowledges and the Chamber believes that the witness has no knowledge of these matters, no basis for these assertions, then this evidence is inadmissible, and the parts that are not conditional on the rules should be stricken from the report. If the Defence is prepared to create a redacted version of the report that removes all matters related to anything other than the de jure structure of the MUP, then perhaps much of my questioning may not be necessary. As long as these de facto matters remain in the report, through, they will be the evidence of this witness. Regardless of what the intention was in creating the report, they need to be tested. The report, and in particular the sections which focus on the role of Franko Simatovic and the JATD, if left the way they are and tendered into evidence without being rebutted, will leave as part of the record not only an incomplete piece of evidence but also unequivocal assertions which, even if partly true, are not the whole truth, even in our view as known by the witness based upon documentation he has reviewed. My cross-examination would focus - and will focus - heavily on the section on Franko Simatovic and the section on the JATD. I will focus on unsourced assertions in the report, the incomplete and, in our view, inaccurate presentation of what the author clearly represents as the status quo at the time, and the omission of what we say the author did know based upon documents he asserted that he reviewed in preparation of his report but did not cite to. In short, our view is that the report is not purely focused on the de jure situation but that it either clearly suggests or explicitly states that the de facto situation was in line with the de jure situation. And in order to do so, the author omits additional information which was at or could have been at his disposal. As we have seen, it is not unusual for the Defence to rely affirmatively upon what is not said, and the fact of that not having been said not only upon what actually is said. Finally, Your Honours, unless the Defence will not be relying upon the report, either its inclusions or its omissions or part of the report in support of its case, the Prosecution submits that we should have a full and fair opportunity to rebut in detail. In particular the sections focused on the accused Simatovic and the JATD. Now, part of that rebuttal, Your Honours, would be through my questioning, and part of it would be through putting certain documents to the witness. If the Chamber prefers that the cross-referencing tools that I have prepared not be used, I have no problem in using that later in submissions. It was a means of making sure that the witness understood how some of the documents I'm going to show to him fit into our case so that he understands clearly the context, and absolutely to be a tool for the Defence and the Chamber to understand what our case is with respect to individual documents that I would put to the witness. The other materials underlying those charts will be tendered by us in rebuttal of the report of this witness because of the submissions that I've just made. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now -- thank you, Ms. Marcus. I should have given you an opportunity earlier, because I do understand that where I instructed you to show that it was the expertise of the witness which you could further explore, that what you are saying is that the witness has not limited himself to -- to the structure, to the rules, to the legislation, but also it was conclusions of a factual nature. I'd like to give an opportunity to the Defence to briefly respond to especially the -- I wouldn't say the shift, but at least the inclusion of the factual parts of the report in the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I may just briefly deal with the issue relating to the JATD and the section of the report which deals with that, and I'll leave the Simatovic team to deal with the issue of Mr. Simatovic. But in relation to the section of the report which deals with the JATD, I don't think my learned friend is right. The witness has been clear that he based his report on the documents. He hasn't asserted that he has factual knowledge of the JATD beyond what the documents say. And the section in his report dealing with the JATD is, as far as I can see, wholly uncontroversial. It doesn't, as far as I can see, assert anything which the Prosecution will, in fact, disagree with. They may say, "Well, he hasn't included things which we know to be the case," but that's not the point. The point is that he's made -- the expert has made assertions about the JATD as far as he is able to according to the documents, and he hasn't made an assertion which the Prosecution, as far as I can see, would disagree with. If that's wrong and they do have a problem with the content of what he said about the JATD, then obviously they're entitled to cross-examine on it. What they're not entitled to do is simply say, "Well, we assert - with no basis whatsoever - that you know all about the JATD, and we're going to prove that by relying upon 48 new documents relating to the JATD in order to assert that you do know about the JATD," and in doing so, elicit a huge amount of fresh evidence. There's no basis for it, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- with all due respect, I haven't commenced my cross-examination on the JATD section yet. I think it's quite premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- I know that. But I think the problem for Mr. Jordash is that you should not start that. Well, whether he's right or wrong, it may depend very much on what questions are put to the witness during cross-examination. First of all, Mr. Petrovic, would you like to add anything to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a few sentences. It's my impression that Mr. Milosevic's position is quite clear. Mr. Milosevic is interpreting the rules and the regulations, the rules of service, in his report. As to whether there are other facts in this case that correspond to what we have heard from him, well, that will be a matter of debate. Mr. Milosevic is not trying to lead us to any conclusions with regard to the facts to decide whether the reality corresponds to the rules and regulations. This is for us to convince the Chamber of the fact. Whether we are successful in doing that, well, we'll see. But that is not what the witness is doing. The witness is providing a normative basis, so he analyses the rules and regulations, but as to situation on the ground, as to the reality whether it is in accordance with the norms and regulations and to what extent, well, the Chamber will decide on the matter. He's interpreting Franko Simatovic's personnel file that the Prosecution has access to. He draws conclusions on the basis of documents. The Chamber has his personnel file, the interpretation of that file, and other evidence. The Chamber will then take its own decision. So what my learned is attempting to do, in my opinion, is an inadequate view of the Defence's intention. The norms are being analysed according to which the service worked, the norms and regulations according to which Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic acted at the time, and everything else is something that concerns the facts. So if my learned friend is disputing his interpretation of the norms, his expertise when it comes to interpreting the norms, if she is going to present some other norms and regulations to him, well, that's fine. But if she wants to show him 45 documents initialed by Mr. Simatovic, well, that just leads us nowhere. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you apparently ignore what Ms. Marcus is saying, that is that the report is not just about rules and regulations. That's part of her submission. Let me just confer with my colleagues for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you have added an element to the discussion of the cross-examination of this witness that you also want to challenge factual parts. Now, first of all, if it is not the factual parts, you can put questions to the witness and elicit evidence -- any evidence which isn't in the realm of his expertise. As far as factual parts are concerned, the Chamber does not yet or would not immediately positively agree with you that what you quoted from the introduction part, whether those claims materialise in the report itself. Nevertheless, the Chamber also understands that you find some factual elements here and there, and the appropriate way of dealing with that is not to put to the witness a lot of material, but first of all to identify exactly what factual portion you are going to deal with; second, then to explore with the witness on what knowledge that factual elements in the report are based. And we'll see after that whether there is any need or whether it assists in putting additional material to the witness. If the witness would show a very flawed basis of his knowledge, which may come down to knowledge not to be taken that seriously, because if he would say, "Well, that's what I thought already on my conversations with my neighbours for the last five years," then I think there would be no need to put specific material, because that would not be a basis on which the Chamber would easily rely and therefore it would not assist the Chamber to hear from the witness that the witness is -- could or could not commence on all kind of material of a totally different nature. Is this sufficient guidance? So we clearly distinguish between expert evidence, then we should limit it to that. If we are going to factual evidence, actual -- factual parts of the report, identify clearly where they are, first explore what the basis of it is, and we'll then decide to what extent it would be appropriate to put other matters to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to show you an example of one of the documents that is contained in this chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P2772 but not broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see before you is a page from the DB personnel file of someone named Milenko Milovanovic. Now, this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go to the signature line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- is signed by Dragoslav Krsmanovic, who you said in your report, at paragraph 375, was the assistant commander of the JATD. This request by Krsmanovic for a background check on 31 candidates for active and reserve duty in the JATD is initialed, we say, at the top by Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could return to the very top so that the signature is visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That is why this is one of the documents on that chart containing documents which we say were signed by or initialed by Mr. Simatovic. My question is: Which aspect of Frenki's official positions and role that you described in paragraph 8 -- sorry, in part eight of your report would have involved signing or initialling documents relating to the JATD?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am not a handwriting expert. I can't confirm that this is his initial. And I'm not familiar with Mr. Simatovic's initials or with his signature. I apologise for laughing a bit. So I can't confirm that it's authentic. But if it is, this could mean two things. It would probably mean that he's familiar with this material. If that's his initial, that was probably the case; he was probably familiar with the material. But I am not aware of all the details. This is the first time I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you focus on what Ms. Marcus clearly asks you. She didn't ask you to verify whether or to tell us whether this is Mr. Simatovic's initials. What she wants to know is what in the description of -- of his job would match with the activity or with the -- would match with being made familiar with a request as the one in this document, that is, the request by Krsmanovic, for a background check on 31 candidates for active and reserve duty in the JATD. Where do we find anything in his job description which would -- which could be matched with this activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These initials mean that he was familiar with this. But I have certain reservations about the initials, so I would have to check whether at the time he was -- I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not asking you to say anything about the initials. Just on an assumption that this, with or without the initials, that this request would have been brought to the attention of Mr. Simatovic at the time the document indicates - that is, in August 1993 - what is it in the job description that would make us understand that this would be brought to the attention of Mr. Simatovic? And just ignore the initials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say exactly. I'd have to have a look at the document. At the time I think he was already the special advisor to the chief. If you allow me to have a look at the documents, I'll answer the question. If he was the advisor, then perhaps that's why his initials are here. The date is the 16th of August, 1993. At the time, he was already the special advisor to the chief of the RDB, so it's quite possible that he had those duties to perform. I have already said that with regard to special advisors, it wasn't known in advance which special advisors would be responsible for certain duties. It was a matter of a specific assignment. And these responsibilities were decided on a case-by-case basis, so this is the only way in which I can understand the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand your answer well, you would say the position of Mr. Simatovic as a special advisor would not make it illogical to keep him informed about this request and to have knowledge of it. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have a request for operational verifications that concerns certain individuals, and this also involves gathering certain intelligence. In Montenegro, intelligence information on place of residence, place of birth, and so on and so forth. And as to the special advisor, he was probably aware of this matter because it's a complex issue and concerned a number of individuals, so he must certainly have been familiar with this case in one way or another. That is my understanding of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's all conclusions, what he certainly must have been familiar with. We leave those conclusions most likely to the Chamber. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Could the Court Officer please call up P2933.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what you will see on the screen in front of you in a moment is an excerpt from the diaries or notebooks of Ratko Mladic. This entry, as you can see, is dated the 16th of December, 1991. In the first line, it says: "Dule Orlovic, Filipovic - Fica and Frenki (Serbia DB/state security/) they want to give some 3.000 barrels to the Muslims in Bihac." For your information, there has been evidence in this case that in this context the word "barrels" means infantry weapons. Perhaps in B/C/S that was clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the 8th of December, 2011, at page 15510.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: Which aspect of Frenki's official position and role, as you describe in paragraph 8 -- sorry, again, in part eight of your report, would have involved providing infantry weapons to the Muslims in Bihac in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no way I can answer this question which only relates to facts. I have no knowledge about anyone delivering anything to anyone or of someone having such tasks on the basis of one's job specifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I again have to interrupt you. The question is not whether this happened. The question is that what is described here, that Frenki - which is a name often used for Mr. Simatovic, but you don't have to bother about that - involved in wishing to give 3.000 barrels to the Muslims in Bihac, whether you, from the point of your expertise, are able to point at any part in the job description or in the description of the function of Mr. Simatovic in December 1991 which would make us understand how this matches to his function. That's the question. And I can imagine that you would first of all look exactly at what his position was in December 1991, and I think what we find about it is primarily in paragraph 364 of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question again is: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood the question, Your Honours. And I did have a look at paragraph 363 and paragraph 364. And in 364 it says that at the time Simatovic was the head of the department for the US intelligence service, so there's no way I can link this to the issue of delivering 3.000 weapons to the Muslims in Bihac. I don't see how this would be part of his job description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I see that I have only a few minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I conclude, Mr. Milosevic, I would like to ask you, please, if you could prepare for us, to the best of your ability, either based on what you remember or perhaps based on some notes or e-mail communications - I don't know - to draw up for us, and if possible - with the Chamber's leave, of course - to provide through the Victim and Witness Section any other documents that you consulted in preparing your report which are not either cited in the footnotes or -- and which are not contained in your bibliography. So I'm referring specifically to a few things that you said. Yesterday, at page 18948, you said: "Based on personnel files and other decisions, including letters of appointments and assignments and the payrolls." Today, at page 7, you said: "There were decisions that concerned Milan Radonjic, and so on and so forth." Today, at page 8 -- I'm sorry, today at page 11, you said: "... I didn't use all the material I had because these are a lot [sic]. For example, on appointments and there are quite a lot of such decisions. It would be absolutely pointless to reference each of those decisions. But if you like, I can try to ..." So, Mr. Milosevic, what I'm asking you - and again, this is only with leave of the Chamber - is to try to the best of your ability to reconstruct which were the other documents that you consulted which you did not provide for in the footnotes or in the bibliography.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, could the witness -- would that be acceptable to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to hear from the Defence whether there are any objections with inviting the witness to try to write down what other sources which we do not find in the report he may have consulted when preparing his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any objections to that. I don't know if it's possible. But I won't go into that. I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we'd like to hear from you, of course. Whether the witness is able to do it ... if he refers to certain materials, then I would expect that at least he would give us some insight in it. But, Mr. Jordash, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Milosevic, would you be willing to dig deep in your memory and see whether -- if you are talking about other personnel files, whether you would remember, for example, how many approximately you've seen - is it in the hundreds, is it five, is it fifty - to try to remember what names you may remember or to try to remember what other decisions you have seen which you may not have used. Are you willing to do it? Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm willing to help in any way I can in order to shed light on the truth, but personnel files aren't concerned here, and mistakes continue to be made here, because here the reference is made to salary lists, but what's concerned are decisions on salaries. That's just a one-page document. Whereas, lists of salaries consist of a lot of pages. Or perhaps the Prosecution doesn't understand me. But the only thing that can be done is to mention key documents that perhaps haven't been mentioned here, and I'll go through the list she shows me to see whether there is anything of significance that could be added. I really don't know exactly how to perform this exercise. This isn't something I could do exhaustively. I could try and identify certain key documents that aided me to draw certain conclusions; for example, the date on which certain units were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm happy that you are willing to offer that assistance, but I'd like to urge you to go a bit further. When I, for example, said, personnel files, whether you remember how many you've seen - and I'm not asking you whether it was 43 or 44 - but I'd like to know whether it's one, or ten, or a hundred, and whether you remember, apart from the personnel file from Mr. Simatovic, whether you remember any names. That, in addition to what you considered to be key documents. And also to think about if it is about decisions on payment, whether you have seen one or two or whether you have seen the whole series of it. Whether you have seen any payrolls. That's -- And again, quantity and the type of document, I take, Ms. Marcus, you are certainly interested in as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you try to do your utmost best not only on what you consider to be the key documents, but also keep in mind what I just added.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. Could we just clarify that the witness would provide that to us in advance of -- not when he comes to court next time perhaps, but as soon as he's ready. Perhaps through the Victim and Witness Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Preparing such a list, Mr. Milosevic, would take you approximately how much time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to say. I really don't know. But there's only one personnel file that is important. It's Franko Simatovic's file. The other documents are only a few decisions. Perhaps by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you say there is only one important, that wasn't the question, which one you considered to be important. What we wanted to know is approximately how many you've seen. If you've seen only Mr. Simatovic's personnel file, then it -- the question is easily answered. If you have seen five, you might remember names or you might not remember names. So don't make your selection on the basis of what you consider to be relevant, but try to be as complete as possible in relation to the type of documents that Ms. Marcus was referring to. Now, let's have a look at the court schedule. If you say could have finished it by Monday morning, then I take it - I'm not intending to spoil your weekend, but there is a Friday in between as well - would you be able to give such a list reflecting, as completely as possible, your reflection on these matters by Monday, well, let's say, 10.00? Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, you've got, then, three days. You are an experienced academic. You would know whether or not you are able to produce that by Monday morning. That's, giving it your best efforts, you just suggested yourself to do it by Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could it be arranged through the Victims and Witness Section that the list could be received from Mr. Milosevic Monday morning, 10.00. Would that serve your purposes? Because we'll adjourn until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day. And I again instruct you, Mr. Milosevic, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony either given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back Tuesday, the 8th of May, at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom, II. And I wish all of you a good weekend. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of May, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
